newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Lafontaine says slumping Kohl must go.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Lafontaine says slumping Kohl must go.

text.p: Oskar Lafontaine, the leader of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), said on Sunday Chancellor Helmut Kohl was a spent force who was slumping in voter surveys because he has run out of ideas.

Lafontaine, in an interview with ZDF television, said the SPD was gaining voter support because it was working together more effectively than in many years and said his party will nominate a candidate in 1998 with the best chance to beat Kohl.

"We need a new political start in Germany and I am convinced that the weak opinion polls for the CDU reflect the fact that people see no chance of a new start with Kohl," Lafontaine said. "They are holding him and his policies responsible for the post-war record levels of unemployment and state debt."
A survey released on Sunday by the Emnid institute found that the SPD leading with 38 percent of the vote compared to 37 percent for Kohl's CDU/CSU.
The Greens, likely coalition partner to the SPD, have 10 percent while Kohl's coalition partners, the FDP, would fail to reenter parliament with just four percent of the vote.

Lafontaine, by saying opinion surveys would play a role in the decision on whether he or Lower Saxony's popular premier Gerhard Schroeder will challenge Kohl, appeared to be signalling his willingness to let Schroeder challenge Kohl.

The pro-business Schroeder consistently beats Kohl in surveys while the chancellor often tops the left-leaning Lafontaine, whom Kohl crushed in the 1990 general elections. The SPD plans to nominate its chancellor candidate in April 1998.
But Lafontaine stopped short of saying Schroeder was the party's man in 1998, saying the would-be candidate's ability to lead the government would play a role in the party's choice.
"The decision (on who will challenge Kohl) will not be made by me or Gerhard Schroeder," Lafontaine said. "It will be a decision made by the party leadership."

He added: "Naturally the opinion polls will play a role as will the candidate's ability to lead the government effectively. And of course the programme will play a role because the government we form should implement the SPD's programme."

In the annual interview with the SPD chairman, Lafontaine declined to comment on remarks made by Schroeder's estranged wife, Hiltrud, who called Schroeder a cheap opportunist. The Schroeders are embroiled in a messy divorce battle that has provided rich fodder for tabloid newspapers.
"I do not in principle comment on private affairs," he said.
But Lafontaine said he did not think Schroeder's divorce problems should be exploited by his political opponents.

"I believe that politicians should stick to the agreement not to intervene in private matters and refrain from dragging them into politics," Lafontaine said. Lafontaine and Schroeder have both been married three times each.

Lafontaine blamed Kohl for the collapse of the tax reform efforts this summer, and said the government should be "ashamed" of itself for reform proposals that would have cut taxes on millionaires by 100,000 marks each year.

"We want a reform where the average household will have its tax burden cut by 2,500 marks," he said. "A reform that would allow Helmut Kohl to save 30,000 marks or would save me 25,000 marks is completely irresponsible and will not become law."
The SPD controls the upper house of parliament and wields the power to block many of the government's iniatives.
Lafontaine said he regretted Kohl's decision to start the election campaign more than a year before the next ballot.

"If he believes the campaign (should begin 14 months) before the next election, then you have to say he is simply overwhelmed in his office," Lafontaine said. "With unemployment as high as it is, you can't just say okay now we'll start the election."
